scope: Subcontinental polities — empires, sultanates, princely states, the colonial regimes (EIC then Raj), and the Republic. Each polity gathers its constitutive events explicitly.

polities.name: Delhi Sultanate
polities.tooltip: Delhi Sultanate — 1206–1526, five Turkic-Afghan dynasties
polities.summary: Three centuries of Turkic-Persian-Afghan rule from Delhi — the Mamluk-Khalji-Tughlaq imperial high water and the long Sayyid-Lodi decline.
polities.framing: The Delhi Sultanate is conventionally read as five distinct dynasties (Mamluk 1206–90, Khalji 1290–1320, Tughlaq 1320–1413, Sayyid 1414–51, Lodi 1451–1526) but ran as one institutional regime — Persian-court, Turkic-military-elite, iqta-funded, with a continuous claim to subcontinental sovereignty backed by an army permanently stationed against the Mongol northwest. The Khalji-Tughlaq high period (1296–1351) was the Sultanate's imperial peak — Alauddin's standing army of 475,000, Malik Kafur's southern campaigns reaching Madurai, the entire subcontinent under tribute. From the Bahmani breakaway (1347) onwards the Sultanate contracted to a north-Indian regional power; Timur's 1398 sack ended the imperial pretension; the Lodi successor regime fell at Panipat in 1526.
rulers: Mamluk: Qutb-ud-din Aibak (1206–1210), Iltutmish (1211–1236), Razia (1236–1240), Balban (1266–1287)
Tughlaq: Ghiyasuddin (1320–1325), Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1325–1351), Firuz Shah (1351–1388)
Sayyid: Khizr Khan (1414–1421), Mubarak Shah, Muhammad Shah, Alam Shah (1445–1451)

sources.label: Peter Jackson, The Delhi Sultanate: A Political and Military History (1999)
Sunil Kumar, The Emergence of the Delhi Sultanate, 1192–1286 (2007)

polities.name: Bahmani Sultanate
polities.tooltip: Bahmani Sultanate — 1347–1527, Deccan breakaway from the Tughlaqs
polities.summary: Hasan Gangu's 1347 revolt produced the first independent Muslim kingdom of the Deccan; fragmented in 1527 into the five Deccan Sultanates.

sources.label: H.K. Sherwani, The Bahmanis of the Deccan (1985)
Richard M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan, 1300–1761 (2005)

polities.name: Sur Empire
polities.tooltip: Sur Empire — 1540–1556, the Suri interregnum between Mughal phases
polities.summary: Sher Shah's 1540 defeat of Humayun inaugurated sixteen years of Suri rule — revenue and road reforms that the returning Mughals inherited intact.

date_span.display: 1540 (Sher Shah defeats Humayun) – 1556 (Hemu falls at Panipat)

sources.label: K.R. Qanungo, Sher Shah and His Times (1965)

polities.name: Mughal Empire
polities.tooltip: Mughal Empire — 1526–1857, Babur's Panipat to formal dissolution after 1857
polities.summary: Babur's victory at Panipat to the formal British dissolution of the empire after 1857 — the longest unified subcontinental imperial regime since the Mauryas.
polities.framing: The Mughal Empire is conventionally periodised in three phases: founding and consolidation (Babur–Humayun–Akbar, 1526–1605), high imperial rule (Jahangir–Shah Jahan–Aurangzeb, 1605–1707), and long decline punctuated by the formal end after the 1857 rebellion. Its institutional legacy — the mansab system, zabt revenue, Persian as administrative language, the Mughal court ceremonial — outlived the dynasty by decades, structuring both the late Maratha Confederacy and the early EIC's Bengal administration. Babur is buried in Kabul; Bahadur Shah Zafar, the last emperor, was exiled to Rangoon and died there in 1862.

date_span.display: 1526–1857 (formal dissolution by EIC after the 1857 rebellion)

rulers: Bahadur Shah I through Bahadur Shah Zafar (1707–1857)

sources.label: John F. Richards, The Mughal Empire (Cambridge New History of India I.5, 1993)
Satish Chandra, Medieval India: From Sultanate to the Mughals — Part Two (1999)

polities.name: Mysore Sultanate
polities.tooltip: Mysore Sultanate — 1761–1799 under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan
polities.summary: Hyder Ali's 1761 coup against the Wodeyar maharaja produced the Mysore Sultanate — four wars against the EIC ended at Tipu's death at Srirangapatna in 1799.

date_span.display: 1761 (Hyder Ali deposes the Wodeyars) – 1799 (Tipu falls at Srirangapatna)

sources.label: Kate Brittlebank, Tipu Sultan's Search for Legitimacy (1997)

polities.name: East India Company
polities.tooltip: EIC — 1600 charter to 1858 dissolution; ruled British India after 1772
polities.summary: Trading company that became colonial state — the EIC ran British India from Hastings's 1772 centralisation until the Crown takeover after 1857.
polities.framing: The East India Company was chartered by Elizabeth I on 31 December 1600 as a joint-stock trading monopoly. The 1757 Plassey victory and the 1765 Diwani grant transferred Bengal's revenue to Company hands; by 1772 Hastings had centralised colonial administration at Calcutta. The Regulating Act (1773) made the Company's Governor-General accountable to the British Parliament; the Charter Acts of 1813 and 1833 stripped its trade monopolies and reduced it to a colonial-administration shell. After the 1857 rebellion the Government of India Act (August 1858) transferred all Company territory to the Crown; the EIC was formally dissolved in 1874. The Company's institutional record — the world's most extensively documented commercial entity by archive volume — is held at the British Library's India Office collections.
rulers: Dalhousie (1848–1856; Doctrine of Lapse, last EIC GG)

sources.label: Philip J. Stern, The Company-State (2011)
William Dalrymple, The Anarchy: The Relentless Rise of the East India Company (2019)

polities.name: British Raj
polities.tooltip: British Raj — 1858–1947, Crown direct rule of India after the EIC
polities.summary: The Crown regime that succeeded the EIC after 1857 — eighty-nine years of direct British rule, ending with the 1947 partition.
polities.framing: The Government of India Act (August 1858) transferred all EIC territory and authority to the British Crown, replacing the Governor-General with a Viceroy answering to the Secretary of State for India in London. The Raj's first half-century (1858–1905) consolidated infrastructure, education, and administrative apparatus; from Curzon's 1905 partition of Bengal onwards it was on the political defensive against an organised Indian nationalism. The 1909 Morley-Minto reforms introduced limited Indian representation; the 1919 Government of India Act (Montagu-Chelmsford) added provincial dyarchy; the 1935 Government of India Act produced the constitutional template the Republic would inherit. The Raj ended at midnight on 14–15 August 1947 with the partition that produced India and Pakistan.

sources.label: Sumit Sarkar, Modern India 1885–1947 (1983)
Bipan Chandra et al., India's Struggle for Independence (1989)
Judith M. Brown, Modern India: The Origins of an Asian Democracy (2nd ed., 1994)

polities.name: Hyderabad State
polities.tooltip: Hyderabad State — 1724–1948, Asaf Jahi (Nizam) dynasty
polities.summary: The largest princely state under British paramountcy — Asaf Jahi rule from the 1724 Mughal-viceroy breakaway to India's 1948 Operation Polo annexation.
rulers: Nizam Ali Khan Asaf Jah II (1762–1803)
Mir Mahbub Ali Khan Asaf Jah VI (1869–1911)
Mir Osman Ali Khan Asaf Jah VII (1911–1948; reportedly the world's wealthiest individual at his height)

sources.label: Karen Leonard, Locating Home: India's Hyderabadis Abroad (2007)
Lucien D. Benichou, From Autocracy to Integration: Political Developments in Hyderabad State 1938–1948 (2000)

polities.name: Khalsa / Sikh Confederacy
polities.tooltip: Khalsa Panth & Sikh political tradition — 1699 founding through 1849
polities.summary: From Guru Gobind Singh's founding of the Khalsa in 1699 to the misls and Ranjit Singh's Sikh Empire — Sikh political tradition through 1849.
polities.framing: The Khalsa was founded by Guru Gobind Singh at Anandpur Sahib on Baisakhi 1699 — a religious-military order that fused initiation through the Five Beloved (Panj Pyare) with armed defence of the Sikh community against Mughal persecution. The earlier Mughal executions of Guru Arjan Dev (1606) and Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675) had radicalised the Sikh tradition; the Khalsa was the institutional response. After Banda Singh Bahadur's brief 1710–15 conquests in Punjab, the Sikh tradition organised through twelve misls (clan-confederacies) through the 18th century, then consolidated under Maharaja Ranjit Singh's Sikh Empire (1801–1849) ruling from Lahore. The Anglo-Sikh wars (1845–46, 1848–49) ended Sikh sovereignty; the East India Company annexed Punjab in 1849.

date_span.display: 1699 (Khalsa founded) – 1849 (annexation of Punjab after the 2nd Anglo-Sikh War)

sources.label: J.S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (Cambridge New History of India II.3, 1990)
Khushwant Singh, A History of the Sikhs (2 vols., 1963; rev. 2004)

polities.name: Maratha Confederacy
polities.tooltip: Maratha Confederacy — Shivaji's coronation 1674 to Anglo-Maratha defeat 1818
polities.summary: Shivaji's 1674 coronation founded the Maratha state; the Confederacy's century of expansion ended at the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–18) defeat by the EIC.
polities.framing: The Maratha state was founded by Shivaji at his coronation at Raigad in 1674 — a deliberate Hindu sovereign-claim against Mughal supremacy in the Deccan. After Shivaji's death (1680) and Sambhaji's execution by Aurangzeb (1689), the Marathas survived twenty-seven years of Mughal pressure, emerging by the 1720s under the Peshwa system as the dominant subcontinental power. At their height (c. 1758) the Maratha Confederacy controlled directly or indirectly most of the subcontinent from Punjab to Karnataka. The Third Battle of Panipat (1761) broke their northern projection; the Anglo-Maratha Wars of 1775–82, 1803–05, and 1817–18 ended Maratha sovereignty. The Peshwa system, the chauth-sardeshmukhi tax structure, and the Mahrashtrian-Konkani administrative tradition the Marathas built persisted into the colonial period.

sources.label: Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600–1818 (Cambridge New History of India II.4, 1993)
Andre Wink, Land and Sovereignty in India: Agrarian Society and Politics under the Eighteenth-Century Maratha Svarajya (1986)

polities.name: Bhopal State
polities.tooltip: Bhopal State — princely state 1723–1949, Begum-rule from 1819
polities.summary: Founded 1723 by an Afghan Mughal-army officer; ruled by four successive Begums 1819–1926 — uniquely a matrilineal princely state.
polities.framing: Bhopal State was founded in 1723 by Dost Muhammad Khan, an Afghan officer of Aurangzeb's army who established himself in the central-India fragment after the post-Aurangzeb collapse. The state's distinctive history began in 1819 when Qudsia Begum took power as regent — the start of more than a century of female succession unique among Indian princely states: Qudsia (1819–1837), Sikandar (1844–1868), Shah Jahan (1868–1901), Sultan Jahan (1901–1926). The Begums modernised Bhopal under British paramountcy — administrative reform, female education, the All-India Muslim Ladies' Conference, the Sultania Girls' School. Bhopal acceded to India in 1949, two years after Sultan Jahan's grandson Hamidullah Khan attempted to remain independent.

sources.label: Shaharyar M. Khan, The Begums of Bhopal: A Dynasty of Women Rulers in Raj India (2000)

polities.name: Travancore
polities.tooltip: Travancore — princely state 1729–1947, Marthanda Varma to accession
polities.summary: Marthanda Varma's 1729 consolidation from Venad; the most administratively reformed and high-literacy princely state under British paramountcy.
polities.framing: Travancore was consolidated in 1729 by Marthanda Varma from the older Venad principality of southern Kerala. His 1750 dedication of the kingdom to Sri Padmanabhaswamy made the rulers nominal regents (dasa) of the deity — a sovereignty-claim that survived British paramountcy. Travancore under successive maharajahs and the Setu Lakshmi Bayi regency (1924–1931) ran among the most administratively reformed princely states — universal primary education for boys from 1817, for girls from 1859, the 1936 Temple Entry Proclamation that opened Hindu temples to all castes after the Vaikom Satyagraha pressure. C.P. Ramaswami Iyer's 1947 attempt to remain independent failed; Travancore acceded to the Indian Union on 27 August 1947 and merged with Cochin in 1949 to form Travancore-Cochin (Kerala from 1956).
rulers: Chithira Thirunal Balarama Varma (1931–1949, last ruling maharaja)

sources.label: Robin Jeffrey, The Decline of Nayar Dominance: Society and Politics in Travancore 1847–1908 (1976)

polities.name: Vijayanagara Empire
polities.tooltip: Vijayanagara Empire — 1336–1646, four dynasties from Hampi
polities.summary: South Indian Hindu empire founded at Hampi by Harihara and Bukka in 1336; broken at Talikota 1565, survived in reduced form to 1646.
polities.framing: Vijayanagara was conceived in the 1330s as the Hindu political-military counter to the Bahmani sultanate (1347) and the Madurai sultanate (1335). Across 310 years and four dynasties — Sangama (1336–1485), Saluva (1485–1505), Tuluva (1505–1570), Aravidu (1570–1646) — the empire ran the longest sustained Hindu-ruled imperial regime in South India after the Cholas. Its peak under Krishna Deva Raya (1509–1529) extended from the Krishna river to Cape Comorin and from the western to the eastern coast. The Talikota defeat of 1565 broke the Hampi-centred empire; the Aravidu dynasty held a reduced state from Penukonda then Chandragiri until 1646. The institutional inheritance — temple-centred land tenure, Telugu-Sanskrit literary patronage, the Nayaka governor system that became the post-Vijayanagara south Indian polities (Madurai, Tanjore, Gingee, Ikkeri) — persisted into the colonial period.
rulers: Sangama: Harihara I (1336–1356), Bukka Raya I (1356–1377)
Tuluva: Krishna Deva Raya (1509–1529, the empire's peak)
Aravidu: Aliya Rama Raya (regent, killed at Talikota 1565)
Aravidu later rulers from Penukonda and Chandragiri (1570–1646)

sources.label: Burton Stein, Vijayanagara (Cambridge New History of India I.2, 1989)

polities.name: Madurai Sultanate
polities.tooltip: Madurai Sultanate — 1335–1378, southernmost Indian Muslim sultanate
polities.summary: Tughlaq-derived breakaway under Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan; eight sultans in 43 years; ended by Vijayanagara reconquest under Kumara Kampana.
rulers: Five further sultans through three decades

sources.label: Mehrdad Shokoohy, Muslim Architecture of South India: The Sultanate of Ma'bar (2003)

polities.name: Bijapur Sultanate
polities.tooltip: Bijapur (Adil Shahi) Sultanate — 1490–1686, Bahmani-successor
polities.summary: Adil Shahi dynasty from Bijapur; longest-lived of the five Bahmani-successor sultanates; annexed by Aurangzeb after 196 years in 1686.
rulers: Ibrahim Adil Shah II (1580–1627; Kitab-i Nauras)

sources.label: Richard M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan (2005)

polities.name: Golconda Sultanate
polities.tooltip: Golconda (Qutb Shahi) Sultanate — 1518–1687, Bahmani-successor
polities.summary: Qutb Shahi dynasty from Golconda then Hyderabad; controlled the Coromandel diamond and textile trade; Aurangzeb annexed in 1687.
rulers: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah (1580–1612; founded Hyderabad 1591)
Abul Hasan Tana Shah (1672–1687, last sultan)

sources.label: Richard M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan (2005)

polities.name: Mysore Kingdom (Wodeyars)
polities.tooltip: Mysore Kingdom — Wodeyar dynasty 1399–1947, with Hyder/Tipu interregnum
polities.summary: Wodeyar dynasty founded 1399; displaced by Hyder Ali 1761; restored by EIC under Krishnaraja III in 1799 as a princely state to 1947.
polities.framing: The Wodeyar (Wadiyar) dynasty was founded at Mysore in 1399 as a Vijayanagara feudatory. After Talikota (1565) the Wodeyars asserted independence, ruling Mysore as a Hindu kingdom for 162 years until 1761, when Hyder Ali — the Wodeyars' Muslim military commander — deposed the maharaja and took power, founding the Mysore Sultanate that ran 1761–1799. After the EIC's 1799 storming of Srirangapatna and Tipu Sultan's death, the EIC restored the five-year-old Krishnaraja III Wodeyar as nominal sovereign under British paramountcy. The 19th-century reformist maharajas (Krishnaraja III, Chamarajendra X, Krishnaraja IV) made Mysore among the most administratively progressive princely states — universal primary education from 1843, the Mysore University (1916), the Krishna Raja Sagara dam, the Mysore Asiatic Pavilion at the 1924 British Empire Exhibition. Mysore acceded to India 9 August 1947 and was reorganised into Karnataka in 1956.
rulers: Raja Wodeyar I (1578–1617; capital shifted to Srirangapatna)
Hyder Ali (1761–1782; Wodeyar deposed, Mysore Sultanate)
Krishnaraja IV (1902–1940), Jayachamaraja (1940–1949, last ruling maharaja)

sources.label: James Manor, Political Change in an Indian State: Mysore 1917–1955 (1977)

polities.name: Ahom Kingdom
polities.tooltip: Ahom Kingdom — 1228–1826, six centuries in upper Assam
polities.summary: Tai-Shan dynasty founded by Sukapha at Charaideo in 1228; ruled upper Assam for 598 years; ended by Burmese invasions and Treaty of Yandabo.
polities.framing: The Ahom kingdom is among the longest continuous regional dynasties in subcontinental history — 598 years from Sukapha's 1228 founding to the 1826 EIC takeover under the Treaty of Yandabo. The Ahoms originated as a small Tai-Shan migration from Mong Mao (modern Yunnan/Myanmar border), assimilated linguistically into Assamese over the 16th–17th centuries, and developed a distinct administrative system: the paik corvée labour structure, the khel occupational guilds, and the buranji historical chronicle tradition (initially in Tai then Assamese). Crucially, the Ahoms repelled seventeen Mughal invasion attempts across the 17th century — the Battle of Saraighat (1671), in which Lachit Borphukan defeated Mirza Raja Ram Singh's Mughal fleet on the Brahmaputra, ended the Mughal effort permanently. The kingdom was destabilised by the Moamoria rebellion (1769–1805) and broken by the Burmese invasions (1817–1826); the EIC takeover ended the dynasty.
rulers: Chakradhwaj Singha (1663–1670; backed Lachit at Saraighat)

sources.label: Edward Gait, A History of Assam (1906; rev. 1933)
Yasmin Saikia, Fragmented Memories: Struggling to be Tai-Ahom in India (2004)

polities.name: Manipur Kingdom
polities.tooltip: Manipur Kingdom — Meitei (Ningthouja) dynasty c. 33 CE through 1949 accession
polities.summary: Meitei (Ningthouja) dynasty by tradition from 33 CE; survived the 1819–26 Burmese Devastation; princely state under EIC paramountcy; acceded to India 1949.
polities.framing: Manipur's Meitei (Ningthouja) ruling lineage is conventionally traced to Pakhangba (33 CE) — among the longest claimed continuous Indian royal lineages. The Manipuri state ran from the Imphal valley with cultural-political reach into the surrounding hills. Vaishnav Hinduism became the court religion under Pamheiba (Garib Niwaz, r. 1709–1748); the Meitei script (Meitei Mayek) and the Sanamahi religion both have ongoing 20th–21st century revival movements. The kingdom was devastated by the Burmese invasion of 1819–1826 (Chahi Taret Khuntakpa); restored by EIC support under Gambhir Singh; survived as a princely state under British paramountcy after the Anglo-Manipur War of 1891 left a child Maharaja under indirect rule. Acceded to India 21 September 1949 under controversial circumstances; statehood 1972; modern Manipur is among the most ethnically contested states in the Indian Union.

date_span.display: Traditional date 33 CE — accession to India 21 September 1949

sources.label: Lal Dena, History of Modern Manipur 1826–1949 (1991)
Gangmumei Kabui, History of Manipur, vol. I: Pre-Colonial Period (1991)

polities.name: Kingdom of Sikkim
polities.tooltip: Kingdom of Sikkim — Namgyal dynasty 1642–1975
polities.summary: Namgyal dynasty consecrated at Yuksom 1642; survived Tibet/Bhutan/Nepal pressure, EIC protectorate (1861), Indian protectorate (1950); merged into India 1975.
polities.framing: The Namgyal dynasty ruled Sikkim for 333 years (1642–1975) — twelve Chogyals from Phuntsog Namgyal to Palden Thondup Namgyal. The kingdom navigated continuous external pressure: Tibetan and Bhutanese raids in the 17th–18th centuries, Nepali (Gorkha) annexation of western Sikkim in 1788, EIC intervention via the 1817 Treaty of Titalia, full British protectorate from 1861, the post-1947 Indian protectorate under the 1950 Treaty. The 1975 referendum (organised by India under controversial circumstances; Indian troops in Gangtok during the vote) abolished the monarchy and merged Sikkim into India as the 22nd state. Sikkim is the only one of the three Himalayan Buddhist kingdoms (Tibet, Bhutan, Sikkim) to lose its sovereignty in the 20th century. The royal dynasty's surviving members live abroad; the institutional record is preserved partly at the Sikkim State Archives, partly in the Namgyal Institute of Tibetology at Gangtok.
rulers: Thutob Namgyal (1874–1914; capital shift to Gangtok)
Palden Thondup Namgyal (1963–1975, 12th and last Chogyal)

sources.label: Saul Mullard, Opening the Hidden Land (2011)
Sunanda K. Datta-Ray, Smash and Grab: Annexation of Sikkim (1984)

polities.name: Tripura Kingdom (Manikya)
polities.tooltip: Tripura Manikya dynasty — 14th c. through 1949 accession
polities.summary: Manikya dynasty from the 14th century; chronicled in the Sanskrit-Bengali Rajmala; tributary then EIC paramountcy; merged into India 15 October 1949.
polities.framing: The Manikya (literally 'jewel') dynasty consolidated rule over Tripura by the 14th century, claiming descent from the lunar dynasty of Mahabharata fame and producing the Rajmala court chronicle commissioned by Maharaja Dharma Manikya in the 1450s — among the few Northeast royal-chronicle traditions in Sanskrit-Bengali rather than indigenous languages. Across regimes the kingdom shifted from Mughal-Bengal nawabi tribute (17th–18th c.), to EIC paramountcy after Plassey (1761), to British Raj paramountcy until 1947. Bir Bikram Kishore Manikya (r. 1923–1947) modernised administration, founded Tripura University, and resisted accession until his death in May 1947. The regency under Kanchan Prabha Devi acceded to India on 15 October 1949. Tripura became a Union Territory then a state (1972). The city of Agartala has been the principal capital since the mid-19th century.

sources.label: Jagadis Gan-Chaudhuri, A Constitutional History of Tripura (1980)

polities.name: Republic of India
polities.tooltip: Republic of India — independent 15 August 1947, republic 26 January 1950
polities.summary: The independent state inaugurated on 15 August 1947 — successor to the British Raj across most of British India and the princely states.

sources.label: Ramachandra Guha, India After Gandhi: The History of the World's Largest Democracy (2007)
